Title: High Precision Conductance Modulation in CuCrP2S6 Synaptic Devices for Enhanced Neuromorphic Computing
Text:
RESEARCH ARTICLE
www.afm-journal.de
High Precision Conductance Modulation in CuCrP2S6
Synaptic Devices for Enhanced Neuromorphic Computing
Xin Cheng, Zhipeng Zhong, Yezhao Zhuang, Wan Wang, Qianyi Yang, Xiang Li, Wu Shi,
Xiangjian Meng, Yanan Cao, Jianlu Wang, Junhao Chu, and Hai Huang*
Artiﬁcial synapses are essential components for realizing neuromorphic
computing at the physical level. Although numerous artiﬁcial synaptic devices
have been fabricated in recent years, their performance is often limited by
their resistance state modulation capabilities and stability. Developing
artiﬁcial synaptic devices with a high number of intermediate states, excellent
linearity, and ultralow power consumption remains a challenge. This work
presents a neuromorphic synaptic device based on a van der Waals layered
ionic conductor material, CuCrP2S6 (CCPS). By precisely controlling the ionic
conductivity of the device, it exhibits exceptional biomimetic synaptic
behaviors, including long-term potentiation (LTP) and depression (LTD) with
up to 8000 intermediate states (13-bit), an exceptional nonlinearity of <0.31,
and operating energy consumption of <45 pJ per pulse. Importantly, the LTP
and LTD behaviors demonstrate outstanding stability, sustaining reliable
modulation over 32 cycles. A convolutional neural network (CNN) based on
the device’s synaptic performance achieves recognition accuracy approaching
full precision simulation in image recognition tasks. Additionally, the device
shows signiﬁcant advantages in processing complex auditory signals,
achieving a recognition accuracy of 96.4% for sound signals, highlighting its
potential in complex sound recognition applications.

ing mechanism, is expected to break through the limitations
of the conventional von Neumann architecture, becoming a

By simulating the neural network struc-

man brain, neuromorphic computing can
achieve eﬃcient parallel computation and

as complex image recognition,[8–17] audio

many eﬀorts have been made to improve
the recognition accuracy of artiﬁcial neural

and enhanced the stability of synaptic de-

in improving the recognition accuracy of

demonstrated the recognition accuracy for handwritten digits in
the MNIST database can be increased from 91.1% to 95.2% when
the number of intermediate states of the long-term potentiation
(LTP) and long-term depression (LTD) behavior increases from

8 to 32. Liu et al.[14] showed increasing the conductance state to
128 (7-bit) could further enhance the recognition accuracy of the
artiﬁcial neural network. However, as the number of resistance
states in the device increases, it may lead to a rise in the nonlinear-
ity of LTP and LTD behaviors, which in turn can cause inhomo-
geneity in the step size during the weight updating, aﬀecting the
ﬁnal recognition accuracy of the artiﬁcial neural network. Krish-
naprasa et al.[15] showed that such issues exist in artiﬁcial synap-
tic devices with a graphene/MoS2/SiOx/Ni structure. These stud-
ies suggest that optimizing the number of intermediate states
while maintaining good linearity under a simple device structure
remains a major challenge. As a result, current synaptic devices
are typically limited to a small number of intermediate states. Ad-
ditionally, due to the limited step size of resistance state modu-
lation, increasing the number of resistance states often leads to
higher operating currents, thus increasing power consumption.
In this study, we developed a two-terminal artiﬁcial synaptic
device based on the ion-conducting van der Waals layered mate-
rial CuCrP2S6 (CCPS). By regulating the ion migration through
applied bias, the two-terminal CCPS device exhibits excellent
neuroplasticity behavior, providing a simple and eﬀective strat-
egy for tuning synaptic performance and emulating the biolog-
ical synapses. Notably, the device achieves a record-high num-
ber of tunable intermediate conductance state up to 13-bit with
a low nonlinearity factor of 0.31, demonstrating outstanding re-
sistance state modulation performance. Furthermore, the device
features ultralow power consumption, reaching as low as 45
pJ/pulse, holds signiﬁcant potential for reducing computational
power consumption. To demonstrate its practical application, we
constructed a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based on this
synaptic device, and achieved eﬃcient recognition of complex
sound signals with a recognition accuracy of 96.4%, approach-
ing the full-precision simulation results of 96.5%. These results
highlight the device’s great potential in speech recognition tasks,
providing a strong foundation for its future integration into arti-
ﬁcial intelligence systems, particularly for energy-eﬃcient com-
puting applications.
2. Results
2.1. Tunable Ionic Conductivity of CCPS Material
CCPS is a van der Waals (vdW) layered material where metal
cations are conﬁned within sulfur-constructed octahedral frame-
works, with interlayer connections maintained by van der Waals
forces. The weak bonding between Cu+ and (P2S6)4−anions
in its molecular structure enables ionic conductivity, eﬀec-
tively mimicking the ion migration behavior between biological
synapses[28–33] (Figure 1a). Artiﬁcial synaptic devices can be fab-
ricated using a simple two-terminal structure as illustrated in
bottom panel of Figure 1a. The device was made by transferring
the mechanical exfoliated CCPS nanoﬂakes onto the Si/SiO2 sub-
strate, followed by the electron beam lithography (EBL), metal de-
position, and lift oﬀprocesses (Experimental Section). The com-
position of the CCPS nanoﬂake was analyzed through the Energy
Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS). Figure 1b shows the SEM image
of the CCPS nanoﬂake along with the corresponding EDS ele-
mental mapping for Cu, Cr, P, and S. The results indicate that

CCPS nanoﬂake. The EDS spectrum conﬁrms the presence of
these elements, with characteristic peaks observed at 0.93 keV
for the Cu L𝛼emission line, 0.573 keV and 5.411 keV for the Cr
L𝛼and K𝛼emission lines, 2.013 keV for the P K𝛼emission line,
and 2.307 keV for the S K𝛼emission line. The atomic ratio of
Cu:Cr:P:S is estimated to be 1:1:2:6 from the EDS spectrum, con-
sistent with the expected stoichiometry of CuCrP2S6, as shown
in Figure 1c.
The representative optical photograph of the CCPS device with
a channel length of 3 μm is shown in Figure 1d, with the thick-
ness proﬁle of the CCPS was characterized through the atomic
force microscopy (AFM). The thickness of the CCPS nanoﬂakes
is determined to be ≈60 nm, as shown in Figure 1e. The ionic
conductivity of CCPS materials was ﬁrstly measured through the
time dependence of the ﬂowing current (I-t) measurements un-
der ﬁxed bias voltages. As shown in Figure 1f, when the applied
voltage is smaller than 0.6 V, the CCPS channel current remains
unchanged with time, which is well acknowledged in the typical
resistor. However, when increasing the bias voltages, it is evident
that the current starts to grow up as a function of time, suggest-
ing the occurring of ionic conductivity in CCPS material. The
threshold electric ﬁeld for the onset of ionic conductivity is ≈2
kV cm−1, indicating larger electric ﬁeld would assist the Cu ion’s
hopping and migration between vacancies or defects. This phe-
nomenon is similar to that observed in CuInP2S6 materials, as
reported before.[34,35] Note that a series of devices made with vary-
ing thickness (ranging from 10 to 80 nm) CCPS nanoﬂakes were
studied, as shown in Figure S1 (Supporting Information). The
threshold electric ﬁeld for the ionic conductivity decreases with
the thickness of the CCPS. Additional Raman spectra character-
ization was also conducted on the CCPS nanoﬂakes,[36,37] show-
ing high quality of the CCPS nanoﬂakes (Figure S2, Supporting
Information).
We further investigated the tunable ionic conductivity of
CCPS-based synaptic device. Through the continuous I-V scan
over 100 cycles on a 60-nm-thick CCPS device, we observed a
progressive increase in conductivity with each scan, indicating
that the ionic conductivity of CCPS material improves over suc-
cessive cycles, as shown in Figure 2a. Additionally, the conductiv-
ity was signiﬁcantly enhanced when the voltage sweeping speed
was reduced from 0.3 to 0.03 V s−1, as depicted in Figure 2b.
Particularly, the hysteresis in conductivity also increases as scan-
ning speed decreased, further supporting the activation of ionic
conductivity.[37–39] We also observed that the ionic conductivity of
the CCPS material varies with the channel length, even though
all devices were fabricated using the same CCPS nanoﬂake with
identical thickness (Figure S3, Supporting Information). This
variation arises because the eﬀective electric ﬁeld increases as the
channel length decreases under the same applied voltage, leading
to diﬀerent degrees of ionic conductivity activation within the ma-
terial (Figure 2c). These results indicate that reducing the chan-
nel length of the CCPS device can eﬀectively lower the required
voltage to initiate ionic conduction.
Furthermore, due to the reversible migration of Cu ions un-
der an electric ﬁeld, the direction of ionic conductivity can be re-

with varying scanning speed show a similar hysteresis behavior
to the positive voltage scans, as depicted in Figure S4 (Support-

and negative conditions, as shown in Figure S5 (Supporting In-

can be reduced to 0.5 V when decreasing the channel length to 0.5
μm, conﬁrming the feasibility of low-voltage operation (Figure
S6, Supporting Information). These results provide important
approaches to regulate the ionic conductivity of the CCPS device.
Lastly, we examined the temperature dependence of the ionic
conductivity by conducting voltage sweeps on the CCPS device
from 250 to 350 K, as shown in Figure 2e. We observed a decrease
in conductivity below 270 K, showing the migration of Cu ions
is signiﬁcantly suppressed at low temperatures. The ﬁtted result
from the Arrhenius plot (𝜎·T verse 1/KB·T) yields an activation
energy of 0.72 eV for Cu’s migration in CCPS (Figure 2f). The
value is very close to that reported in bulk materials.[29,40]
2.2. Performance of CCPS Synaptic Devices
Since the conductivity of CCPS device is primarily governed by
the ion migration under high electric ﬁeld, it can be regulated
through various parameters, such as the electric ﬁeld, scanning
speed, and voltage duration. We further investigated the neuro-
plasticity behavior of the CCPS device. As shown in Figure 3a, the
application of a 10 V bias pulse induces a temporary increase in
the device’s conductivity, exhibiting short-term plasticity (STP).
This enhancement is transient, with conductivity rapidly return-
ing to its original state after the pulse. However, repeated volt-
age pulses lead to a more permanent enhancement in conductiv-
ity, resulting in the long-term plasticity (LTP). The paired-pulse
facilitation (PPF) index, deﬁned as the ratio of conductivity af-
ter the second pulse (A2) to the ﬁrst pulse (A1), is sensitive to
the time interval between pulses.[41] As shown in Figure 3b, a
larger PPF of 165% is achieved with a shorter interval of 0.2 s.
The decay of PPF with increasing interval time (Δt) follows a
double-exponential function:PPF(Δt) = C0 + C1 ⋅exp(−Δt∕𝜏1) +
C2 ⋅exp(−Δt∕𝜏2). The constant 𝜏1 and 𝜏2 represent the character-
istic relaxation times of the fast and slow phases, reﬂecting the
rate of learning in biological synapses. The ﬁtted results, 𝜏1 and
𝜏2 are 0.38 and 3.8 s, respectively, and 𝜏2 is an order of magni-
tude larger than 𝜏1, which closely resembles biological synaptic
behavior.[41,42] Figure 3c–e demonstrate the inﬂuence of voltage
pulse number, pulse duration, and pulse amplitude on the CCPS
synaptic device’s conductivity. As seen in Figure 3c, the conduc-
tivity increases monotonically with the number of voltage pulses,
where a 10 V bias pulse with a duration of 2 s is used to stimulate
the ionic conductivity, and a 1 V read voltage is applied to measure
the postsynaptic current. In Figure 3d, conductivity is observed
to increase monotonically as the pulse duration extends from 1 to
4 s after ﬁve pulses. Similarly, as shown in Figure 3e, increasing
the pulse amplitude from 3 V to 15 V results in a corresponding
increase in conductivity, while the read voltage remains ﬁxed at
1 V. These results resemble synaptic plasticity in biological neu-
ral networks, where frequent, prolonged, and stronger stimuli
lead to enhanced connectivity between neurons, increasing the
excitability of postsynaptic neurons. Notably, synaptic regulation
behavior can also be observed with individual pulses of varying
amplitude and duration, as shown in Figure S7 (Supporting In-
formation).
The CCPS device not only demonstrates tunable STP and LTP
behavior, but also shows an inhibition phenomenon under elec-
tric pulses. As shown in Figure 3f, applying a −5 V voltage pulse
drives Cu ions in the opposite direction, resulting in a suppres-
sion of the conductivity when measured at 1 V. This pulse appli-
cation induces short-term depression (STD) with a single pulse
and long-term depression (LTD) with continuous pulses. Fur-
thermore, the degree of conductivity depression can be modu-
lated by adjusting the number of applied pulses. As illustrated
in Figure 3g, as the pulse count increases from 5 to 15, the con-
ductivity measured at 1 V decreases in a monotonic manner. Ad-
ditionally, the inﬂuence of pulse amplitude and pulse number
on the CCPS device can also eﬀectively simulate the emotional
threshold reactions behavior, as shown in Figure S8 (Supporting
Information). These ﬁndings suggest that the CCPS device holds
promise as a synaptic element for neuromorphic computing ap-
plications.
Next, we aimed to increase the number of the intermediate
states within the LTP and LTD behaviors. To induce LTP, a 3 V
voltage pulse was applied to drive ion migration, while the con-
ductivity was read at 1 V after the pulse, with the pulse duration
shortened to 0.25 s. Under this condition, up to 8000 interme-
diate states (approximately 13-bit) were achieved in the LTP be-
havior of the CCPS device (Figure 4a; Figure S9, Supporting In-
formation). During this process, the operation current increased
from 23 pA to 94 pA, with the low operation current ensuring
the low power consumption during the states updating.[16] The
energy consumption (E) for each pulse is ≈45 pJ, deﬁned as E =
Vb × I × t, where Vb, I, and t are the programing voltage, and cor-
responding current, and pulse duration, respectively.[43,44] Simi-
larly, by applying a −1 V voltage pulse with a duration of 0.15 s
to stimuli the Cu’s migration and read the conductivity at 1 V,
LTD behavior with 8000 intermediate states was also achieved
(Figure 4b; Figure S10, Supporting Information). Figure 4c,d
show the LTP and LTD curves extracted from the conductance
state at 1V. The nonlinearity factors (NLF) for the LTP and LTD
curves are calculated to be 0.31 and 2, respectively, with de-
tailed calculation procedures described in Experimental Section.
Figure 4e shows the variation of the NLF for the LTP process as
the number of states increases. As seen, the nonlinearity factor
remains relatively low even as the number of states increases.
Additionally, we compare the NLF and the number of interme-
diate states with previous works that also aimed to increase the
number of states in synaptic devices.[13–15] It is evident that our
results not only surpass previous works in the number of inter-
mediate states but also achieve a lower NLF compared to these
studies. The comparison of the NLF during the LTD process with
these materials is demonstrated in Figure S11 (Supporting In-
formation), further demonstrates the superior performance of
our device. Moreover, the LTP and LTD behavior exhibit high
stability after 32 cycles of measurements, which involved over
35 000 voltage pulses in total, as shown in Figure 4f. The LTP
and LTD behavior was also investigated across 18 independent

2.3. Voice Recognition Using the CCPS-Based Synaptic Devices
Sounds recognition is an important topic in the ﬁelds of artiﬁcial
intelligence and human-computer interaction. The goal of sound
recognition is to emulate the human auditory system by extract-
ing and identifying meaningful information from noisy and di-
verse sound environments and making judgments about the au-
dio signals[45–47] (Figure 5a). Additionally, it aims to surpass the
human auditory system by incorporating a more extensive knowl-
edge base and greater stability. However, achieving high accu-
racy in audio recognition and keyword spotting in complex en-
vironments remains a major challenge, which places extremely
high demands on the accuracy of artiﬁcial neural networks. Given
the excellent characteristics of the CCPS synaptic device, we at-
tempted to apply it in the ﬁeld of voice recognition.[20]
Inspired by the human auditory system, we developed a con-
volutional neural network (CNN) based on the CCPS synaptic
devices for voice recognition (Figure 5b). This biomimetic audi-
tory system is speciﬁcally designed for voice recognition tasks.
Speech commands for digits “0” to “9” were selected from the
Google Speech Commands dataset, and Mel-frequency cepstral
coeﬃcient (MFCC) features were extracted and fed into the CNN,
which consists of three convolutional layers and three pooling
layers. This architecture eﬀectively captures the time-frequency
characteristics of speech signal while reducing computational
complexity. The LTP and LTD curves of the CCPS device were
extracted, and the normalized current values were mapped to a
range of −1 to 1 to represent synaptic weights. After each train-
ing round, the weights were adjusted based on the training out-
comes. After 100 epochs of training, the system achieved a speech
recognition accuracy of over 96.4%, approaching the 96.5% ac-
curacy achieved through full-precision simulation, as shown in
Figure 5c. To further evaluate the system’s performance, we con-
ducted a detailed analysis of recognition accuracy for individual
digits (“0” to “9”). The accuracy gap between the CCPS device
and full-precision simulation remained within a 0.03% margin,
as shown in Figure 5d. The recognition accuracy for spoken digits
is also compared with prior works in Table 1, highlighting the re-
markable performance of the CCPS device-based CNN. These re-
sults demonstrate that the neuromorphic acoustic system based
on CCPS devices exhibits signiﬁcant potential for complex acous-
tic scene recognition, keyword spotting, and broader applications
such as smart security and traﬃc monitoring.[48–52]
3. Conclusion
In this study, we explored the regulation of ionic conductivity in
two-terminal CCPS synaptic device, demonstrating its potential
for high-accuracy neuromorphic computing. The CCPS synap-
tic device operates at ultralow current of 23 pA with low power
consumption <45 pJ/pulse, enabling the high energy eﬃciency
in neuromorphic computing. By precisely tuning the ionic con-
ductivity, the CCPS device achieves up to 8000 (13-bit) tunable
conductance states with highly linear LTP and LTD behavior. Fur-
thermore, the LTP and LTD behavior show high stability after
32 cycles of measurements, totally modulated by over 35 000
voltage pulses. These properties enable the CCPS synaptic de-
vice to exhibit exceptional performance in neuromorphic com-
puting. Leveraging its synaptic behavior, a CNN network based
on CCPS devices achieves a recognition accuracy of up to 98.85%
for the MNIST dataset and 92% for the Fashion-MNIST dataset,
approaching the full-precision simulation. Furthermore, its out-
standing performance is demonstrated in complex audio signal

4. Experimental Section
Device
Fabrication
and
Characterization:
CCPS
nanoﬂakes
were
cleaved from bulk crystal purchased from Shenzhen six carbon Semicon-
ductor Technology company using mechanical exfoliation method and
then transferred to the silicon substrate with 285 nm oxidation layer. The
Cr/Au electrodes with thickness of 10/50 nm were grown through the
thermal evaporation, followed by the electron beam lithography (EBL).
Lift-oﬀprocesses were conducted to complete the device structure.
Devices made with diﬀerent thicknesses 10, 40, 60, and 80 nm with
channel length ranging from 3 to 35 μm were investigated in this work.
The thickness of the CCPS nanoﬂakes was characterized by the AFM
(Dimension ICON). Raman spectroscopy of the CCPS nanoﬂakes was also
characterized on the device using a laser confocal Raman spectrometer
(Renishaw, 532 nm excitation laser). The electrical characteristics of the
CIPS device were measured in a lakeshore vacuum probe station using the
Keithley 4200 and Keysight B1500A semiconductor parameter analyzer.

Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) Based on the Device Data for Image
and Voice Recognition:
The study constructed a convolutional neural net-
work (CNN) to test image recognition capabilities using the MNIST and
Fashion MNIST dataset. The CNN consists of an input layer, a convolu-
tional layer with a 3 × 3 kernel, a max-pooling layer, and two fully connected
layers, with the ﬁnal output layer using a softmax activation function to
classify into ten categories. The MNIST dataset includes 60 000 training
images and 10 000 test images, each 28 × 28 pixels, representing hand-
written digits (0-9). Similarly, the Fashion MNIST dataset contains 60 000
training and 10 000 test images, each 28 × 28 pixels, labeled across ten
fashion categories. Both datasets use grayscale images with pixel values
ranging from 0 to 255. During training, the CNN adjusts its weights, uti-
lizing the normalized conductance states of the LTP and LTD properties
derived from a CCPS device. The image recognition accuracy based on the
CCPS device data for the MNIST dataset reaches 98.85%, and for Fash-
ion MNIST dataset reaches 92.04%, closely approaching the full-precision
simulation results of 98.99%, and 92.27%, respectively.
Voice recognition was tested using the Google Speech Commands
dataset, which includes digits 0 to 9 and other common voice commands.
The dataset features samples from diverse genders, ages, and accents,
recorded at a 16 kHz sampling rate. The digit commands (0-9) are padded
to 1 second, and Mel-frequency cepstral coeﬃcients (MFCC) are extracted
as features. These features are input into a convolutional neural network
(CNN) with three convolutional and pooling layers. Dropout is applied af-
ter each convolutional block to prevent overﬁtting. After the convolutional
layers, a fully connected layer performs classiﬁcation using a softmax acti-
vation function. The weights for both the convolutional and fully connected
layers are represented by the normalized conductance values of the LTP
and LTD characteristics of CCPS devices. The model is trained with the
ADAM optimizer, a batch size of 1000, and a learning rate of 0.001, achiev-
ing an accuracy of ≈96.4%, which is nearly identical to the full-precision
CNN simulation result of 96.5%. To assess robustness under hardware
imperfections, multiplicative Gaussian noise (0.1-20%) was applied to the
mapped weights, along with ﬁxed mapping noise (0.005) and drift (0.001)
(Figure S16, Supporting Information). The CNNs maintained >95% accu-
racy under moderate noise (≤5%), demonstrating strong noise resilience
and application potential of CCPS-based neuromorphic systems.
